verdicts.reason: The left ventricle is part of the heart (SNOMED heart structure subsumes it), and 'heart pumping at 25 percent' is the lay way to report LV ejection fraction.
'Poop transplant' is the common lay name for fecal microbiota transplant.
'Parkinson's pills' names the antiparkinson drug class, which contains carbidopa-levodopa and truly describes it here.
A 'funny feeling before my seizures' is the standard lay paraphrase of an epileptic aura, a subjective warning sensation before a seizure.
The wrist is the body region of the access site, not the vessel. The radial artery runs through the forearm and wrist and is neither a kind of wrist nor wholly part of it.
'Upset stomach' is the consumer synonym for dyspepsia, or indigestion (MedlinePlus), and the post-meal context fits.
Norvasc is the brand name of single-ingredient amlodipine.
'Throwing up' is the standard consumer synonym for vomiting.
Tums is a calcium carbonate antacid, a different drug from pancrelipase (Creon, Zenpep); people do say 'my Tums', but not for enzymes.
'Shot' covers injected medication in general (RxNorm injectable product), and self-injected adalimumab falls within it, so 'my shot' names the missed dose less specifically.
'The pink stuff' is the well-known nickname for Pepto-Bismol (bismuth subsalicylate). It is a nickname rather than a brand name, and the black stool settles which drug is meant.
'Nausea medicine' names the antiemetic class, which contains ondansetron.
Getting out of breath on exertion is the consumer description of dyspnea (shortness of breath).
Metamucil is the brand of single-ingredient psyllium husk fiber.
'Memory pill' is the lay name for the class of dementia and memory drugs, which contains donepezil.
The aortic valve is a heart valve (parent concept), so 'replaced my heart valve' truly describes it.
Lactaid pills are the brand of single-ingredient lactase enzyme; the word 'pills' rules out Lactaid milk.
The right upper quadrant is part of the right side of the abdomen, so 'right side' places the biliary pain correctly but less precisely.
Imodium is the brand of single-ingredient loperamide.
'Blood in my poop' is the consumer phrasing for visible blood in the stool, which is hematochezia; patients describe melena separately as black stool.
'Blood thinner' names the anticoagulant class, which contains warfarin.
Aricept is the brand name of single-ingredient donepezil.
'Water pill' is the MedlinePlus lay name for diuretics, a class that contains furosemide.
Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing (MedlinePlus); 'trouble swallowing' is the consumer synonym.
'Puking' is a colloquial synonym for vomiting.
After a blow to the head, 'blacked out' is the lay synonym for losing consciousness.
The chest is a body region, not a valve; 'they replaced my chest' is false and is not something a patient would say.
'The blues' is transient low mood, which consumer health sources explicitly distinguish from clinical depression, a disorder.
The small intestine is a kind of intestine (parent concept), so 'intestines' correctly but less precisely names the site of the bacterial overgrowth (SIBO).
'Infusion' covers IV-infused treatment in general, and infliximab is given by IV infusion every 8 weeks, so 'my infusion' names the same dose less specifically.
Diaphoretic means sweating profusely; 'sweating buckets' is the idiomatic lay paraphrase of that definition.
Tachycardia is a fast heart rate, while central chest pain is a different symptom; 'My pain in the middle of my chest' also doubles the possessive awkwardly.
Mestinon is the brand name of single-ingredient pyridostigmine bromide.
Humira is the originator brand of single-ingredient adalimumab.
Botox is the brand name of onabotulinumtoxinA, which is approved for chronic migraine.
Lyrica is the brand name of single-ingredient pregabalin.
In Southern US and African American English, 'falling out' means fainting or passing out, the lay term for syncope; without 'with', the quarrel reading does not fit the sentence.

'Nerve pain' is the consumer synonym for neuropathic pain; both are entry terms under MeSH Neuralgia.

'Ticker' is slang for the heart, the whole organ containing the left ventricle (LV structure is-a heart structure in SNOMED); 'my heart pumps at 25 percent' is the usual lay statement of LVEF.

'Migraine pills' is a functional drug category (triptans, NSAIDs, others) that contains sumatriptan tablets.
'Puffer' is the common Commonwealth colloquial synonym for an inhaler.
Dizziness is the parent concept of vertigo (in SNOMED, vertigo is-a dizziness); 'dizzy spells' loses the spinning specificity but still describes vertigo episodes.
'Heartburn pills' covers antacids, H2 blockers and PPIs, a functional category that contains omeprazole.

A plain paraphrase of the definition: pleuritic pain is chest pain that worsens when breathing in.

'Cholesterol pill' is the lay name for the lipid-lowering class that contains atorvastatin.

'Cholesterol pills' names the lipid-lowering class that contains atorvastatin.

The atrial septum is the wall between the heart's upper chambers (a hole there is an ASD or PFO), while 'main artery' means the aorta. The structure is different, and the patient term looks copied from c0084.
'Blackout' is the lay term for transient loss of consciousness (as in the NICE guideline), which contains syncope and still describes this episode.
'Heart arteries' is a plain paraphrase of the coronary arteries.

Belly is the standard consumer synonym for abdomen, and both read naturally in this sentence about fluid building up (ascites).

Consumer sources (AHA, Mayo) describe claudication as painful leg cramping brought on by walking. 'Leg cramps' is the broader lay category, and the walking trigger makes it truly describe claudication. Strictly, a muscle cramp in MeSH is a different mechanism.
Sac around my heart is a plain paraphrase of the definition of the pericardium (the sac surrounding the heart).
The chest is the region that contains the sternum, and 'split my chest for the bypass' truly describes a median sternotomy.
'Enzymes' is what patients call pancreatic enzyme replacement, the class that pancrelipase belongs to, so it truly describes the drug.
Dilantin is the brand name of single-ingredient phenytoin.
MedlinePlus lists dyspepsia and upset stomach as alternative names for indigestion.

Micrographia is abnormally small handwriting, which 'tiny handwriting' directly paraphrases.
Diaphoretic means sweating profusely, and 'dripping with sweat' is a plain paraphrase of that.
Arteries is the parent concept of coronary arteries and still truly describes the blocked vessel that is getting a stent.

The semicircular canals are part of the inner ear (inner ear structure subsumes them in SNOMED), so the containing structure still truly locates the loose crystals.

Creon is a brand of pancrelipase, the FDA established name of its single active drug substance.
The cubital tunnel lies entirely within the elbow region, so 'elbow' is its containing region and truly locates the pinched nerve.

Stool softeners is the drug class that contains docusate (MedlinePlus describes docusate as a stool softener).
The elbow is a joint region and the ulnar nerve is a nerve that passes by it; the pair swaps the place being pressed for the nerve being compressed, and neither is a parent of the other.

A plain paraphrase of chest pain radiating to the left arm.

'Bowel' means the intestines (MeSH Intestines > Intestine, Large > Colon), so it contains the colon.

'Steroids' (corticosteroids) is the drug class that contains methylprednisolone.
'Dope sick' is the street term for opioid withdrawal; 'getting opioid withdrawal' is an awkward collocation where 'getting dope sick' is idiomatic.
'Backed up' is a colloquial synonym for constipated.
The ear contains the semicircular canals (inner ear); 'crystals in my ear' is the standard lay description of BPPV.

'Accidents' is a euphemism for incontinence episodes of either the bladder or the bowel, which includes fecal incontinence.

Coumadin is a brand name of single-ingredient warfarin, and patients still use that name for it.
'Accidents' is the common euphemism for incontinence episodes of bladder or bowel, so it covers fecal incontinence but does not say which kind.
'The crud' is slang for a vaguely defined minor illness, usually respiratory; it truly covers bronchitis but is much less specific.
Keppra is levetiracetam, a seizure drug; clopidogrel's brand is Plavix, so this names a different drug, even though patients do say 'Keppra'.
Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor used for blood pressure; 'blood pressure pill' names the drug class that contains it.
The 'pit of the stomach' is the everyday name for the epigastrium, so this phrase restates epigastric pain.
'Baby aspirin' is the standard consumer name for low-dose (81 mg) aspirin.
The saphenous vein is the leg vein taken for bypass grafts; 'vein from my leg' is less specific but still accurate.
'Tummy' is a consumer synonym for the abdomen; NHS material writes 'tummy (abdomen)'.
'The spins' is the everyday name for the spinning sensation that defines vertigo.
'Side' alone gives no left or right, and consumer usage maps 'side pain' to flank pain, a region that overlaps the right upper quadrant without containing it.
MedlinePlus describes the atrial septum as the wall between the heart's upper chambers; 'wall of my heart' drops which chambers but still describes it accurately.
In 'bleeding from my ___', 'butt' means the lay 'bottom' (NHS: bleeding from the bottom = rectal bleeding); it does not separate anus from rectum but correctly names the site.
The right side of the abdomen contains the right upper quadrant, and consumer sources describe gallbladder pain this way (NHS: 'under the ribs on your right side').
MedlinePlus defines the aorta as the main artery, so 'main artery' restates the definition; it reads as leaflet wording, and people more often just say 'aorta'.
The peroneal nerve is a leg nerve often compressed by crossing the legs; 'nerve in my leg' is less specific but still accurate.
Photophobia is eye discomfort in bright light (MedlinePlus); 'can't stand bright light' says the same thing in plain words.
AAOS patient material says the spot where the ulnar nerve runs through the cubital tunnel, under the medial epicondyle, is commonly called the 'funny bone', so both name the same place.
